summary: Yemen requires an embassy visa obtained in advance for virtually every nationality — there is no eVisa or visa on arrival — and mainland tourist visas are rarely issued while the armed conflict continues. Organized tourism survives only on the island of Socotra, where licensed operators arrange the visa as part of a package.

travelInsurance.text: No insurance is checked at the border, but comprehensive coverage including medical evacuation is essential, and most mainstream insurers exclude Yemen entirely because of the active conflict, so specialist cover is usually needed.

notes: Alcohol may not be brought into Yemen. It is prohibited and will be confiscated.
Drones and professional camera gear attract heavy scrutiny; photographing checkpoints, military sites or infrastructure can lead to detention.

payments.text: Yemen is a cash economy — international cards are almost unusable and ATMs unreliable, so bring US dollars in cash to exchange. Two rival central banks mean exchange rates differ sharply between Sana'a- and Aden-controlled areas.

safety.text: Yemen remains in active armed conflict and virtually all governments advise against all travel: risks include airstrikes and fighting, landmines, kidnapping and terrorism, and consular help is effectively unavailable. The island of Socotra is calmer than the mainland but is reached only on limited flights.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Yemen Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: October to April is the most temperate window and the main Socotra season. The island is largely cut off by monsoon winds from June to September.

tips.text: Virtually all governments advise against all travel to Yemen because of the armed conflict, kidnapping and terrorism risk; embassies of most countries are closed and cannot help you. Any travel requires professional security arrangements.

Socotra is the one part of Yemen with organized tourism — licensed operators arrange the visa and seats on the limited flights (usually via Abu Dhabi). The visa covers the island only and is not valid for the mainland.

Yemen is split between rival administrations — paperwork issued for Sana'a-controlled areas may not be honored in Aden-controlled areas and vice versa, so your sponsor or operator must match your point of entry.
Bring everything you plan to spend as cash — US dollars are the most exchangeable; cards and international ATMs do not work.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Yemen?
faq.answer: Yes — apart from Gulf Cooperation Council citizens, every nationality needs a visa obtained in advance from a Yemeni embassy. There is no eVisa or visa on arrival, and mainland tourist visas are rarely granted while the conflict continues.

faq.question: Is it safe to visit Yemen?
faq.answer: No. Yemen is in active armed conflict and Western governments uniformly advise against all travel, citing airstrikes, kidnapping, terrorism and landmines. Consular assistance is effectively unavailable inside the country.

faq.question: Can tourists still visit Socotra?
faq.answer: Yes — Socotra island runs a small, separate tourism circuit. Licensed tour operators obtain the entry visa on your behalf and book the limited flights, usually via Abu Dhabi. The permit is valid for the island only, not the Yemeni mainland.

faq.question: Does Yemen have an eVisa or visa on arrival?
faq.answer: No. All visas are issued in advance through Yemeni embassies or, for Socotra, arranged by licensed tour operators before you fly.

faq.question: Can I enter Yemen with an Israeli passport or Israeli stamps?
faq.answer: No — Israeli passport holders are not admitted, and evidence of travel to Israel in any passport can also lead to refusal of entry.
